narrative: Your promotion was denied because the model estimates a 96% probability that you will leave your job. In practical terms, the model sees leaving as highly likely, so the organization treated a promotion as an investment at serious risk of being lost. The strongest signal was your total work experience: you have 11 or more years overall, a level found among only about 15% of employees predicted to stay. That long track record, combined with the second-strongest signal—that you already have other job opportunities—made leaving more likely; most employees predicted to stay reported no such opportunities. Your tenure in the current organization, between one and five years, was the third most influential factor and also pushed the prediction toward leaving, though it is common among stayers too. The model also saw a profile that can reinforce turnover risk: no bonus, no recognition, low job support, low environment satisfaction, and not feeling you received the promotion you deserved. Next, the organization should discuss your opportunities and promotion expectations openly and address recognition, support, and satisfaction; you should clarify what would keep you engaged. A promotion decision should not rest on the prediction alone.
